newsitem.title: MEXICO: Investors may have miscalculated Mexico upset.
newsitem.headline: Investors may have miscalculated Mexico upset.

text.p: Investors may have underestimated the impact of left-winger Cuauhtemoc Cardenas becoming mayor of Mexico's capital city, economists said on Monday.

Investors had dismissed a Cardenas victory, arguing that the post of mayor carried little real national clout, and Mexican financial markets rallied in the month leading up to Sunday's first free election in the city.

But economists say Mexico's political landscape has changed after results showed Cardenas won nearly half the city's vote, while his Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) make unexpectedly big gains in the election of a new lower house of Congress.
"My view is that the Mexico City race is a little more important than people have portrayed it," said Gray Newman, chief economist for HSBC James Capel here.
"Power is not derived from an individual's job description, it's an ability to become a spokesman for various interests, and he has the chance now to do an awful lot."

By winning nearly half the city's votes, almost twice as much as his ruling party rival, Cardenas won a huge power base and a platform to influence Mexico's political and economic agenda, analysts said.
"(The vote) has given him a very strong mandate," said Rogelio Ramirez del la O, director of Mexico City-based economic advisors Ecanal.
"He will turn that into permission to speak out very clearly on issues natural to him," he said.

Though he has no power to change policy singlehandedly, the veteran politician is likely to use his party's gains in the lower house to press his economic agenda and win support ahead of the 2000 presidential race.

"Even though his position does not strictly have influence at the national level, he will do that through Congress and through setting the line for a populist position that the other parties will have to follow or suffer an important political cost," said Sergio Martin at ING Barings here.

Economists took fright during the election campaign when Cardenas spoke out against Mexico's new private pension fund system, and many fear he could stall further progress on Mexico's economic reforms.
Cardenas nearly won the presidency in 1988 by calling for a renegotiation of the country's foreign debt, but has since toned down some of his more radical left-wing proposals.

However, he still proposes some ideas that rankle conservative economists. The PRD economic platform calls for a greater budget deficit to boost employment, a tax on short-term foreign investment and curbs on the independence of the central bank.

While economists said voters have not all opted for the left, they have voted against the PRI for presiding over an economic crisis that saw real wages drop by 30 percent since 1995, and an austerity programme that failed to deliver any palpable recovery in their standard of living.
With an eye on the 2000 race, Congressional parties may well toe a slightly more populist line from now on.
"What's most important here is that the Congress (from now on) will be shy of economic reform," ING Barings' Martin said.
Ramirez de la O said uncertainty was unlikely to set in until later in the year.
"From October to December I think we will see tension build up," he said, but added that markets would remain bullish until then.
The federal budget has to be passed by November 15 and Cardenas will formally take office on December 5. Mexico City's budget also has to be negotiated at about that time.
